In an organic-synthesis lab, when a chemist says that “the compounds are on top of each other,” the usual context is chromatography or TLC analysis.  
If two substances travel the plate or the column at essentially the same rate, their spots/bands appear at the same position – literally one “on top of” the other – so they cannot be separated.  
The reason compounds co-elute like this is that they have very similar polarities, giving them the same affinity for the stationary and mobile phases.

A. Similar boiling points → problem in a distillation, not described as “on top of each other.”  
B. Similar optical rotations → affects polarimetry, not separation.  
C. Non-covalent bonding between molecules → might alter behavior, but “on top of each other” is not the standard expression.  
D. Similar polarities → gives identical Rf values/co-elution; this is exactly what “on top of each other” refers to in routine lab talk.

Answer: D
